name: Ezekiel
v: The word of the LORD hit me again:
Son of man, make Jerusalem face what she is. Show her every disgusting thing she's done.
Tell her: This is what the Lord GOD says to Jerusalem — Your roots, your birth, are Canaanite soil. Your father was an Amorite. Your mother, a Hittite.
The day you were born, no one cut your cord. No one washed you clean. No one rubbed you with salt or wrapped you in cloth.
No eye looked at you with pity. No hand reached for you to do even one of these things. They threw you out in an open field, repulsed by the sight of you, on the day you were born.
Then I came by. I saw you kicking in your own blood. And I said to you, lying there in that blood — Live. I said it again — Live.
I made you flourish like a wildflower. You grew. You bloomed. You became a woman — breasts formed, hair grew long — but you were still naked, still bare.

I came by again. I looked at you. You were ready for love. So I spread the corner of my cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I gave you my oath. I entered a covenant with you — the declaration of the Lord GOD — and you became mine.
I washed you. I rinsed the blood off your skin. I anointed you with oil.
I dressed you in embroidered linen, gave you leather sandals, wrapped you in fine cloth, draped you in silk.
I covered you in jewelry — bracelets on your wrists, a chain around your neck,
a ring in your nose, earrings in your ears, a crown of beauty on your head.
Gold and silver were your ornaments. Your clothes were linen and silk and embroidery. You ate the finest flour, honey, oil. You became staggeringly beautiful — fit to be queen.
Your name went out among the nations because of your beauty. It was perfect — because the splendor I had placed on you made it so. The declaration of the Lord GOD.
But you trusted in your beauty. You traded on your fame and turned whore. You poured your seductions out on every passerby — anyone who walked by could have you.
You took your clothes and made bright-colored shrines out of them, and there you played the whore. Nothing like this has ever happened — nothing like this should ever happen.
You took the beautiful jewelry I gave you — my gold, my silver — and you molded yourself male images and prostituted yourself to them.
You took your embroidered robes and dressed those idols in them. My oil, my incense — you set them before those things.
The food I provided you — the fine flour, the oil, the honey I put in your mouth — you set before them as a sweet aroma. That's what happened. The declaration of the Lord GOD.
You took your sons and your daughters — the children you bore to me — and sacrificed them to those things to be devoured. As if your prostitution wasn't enough,
you butchered my children and handed them over, burning them up as offerings.
In all your obscenities and whoring, you never once remembered the days of your youth — how you were naked and bare, kicking in your own blood.
And then — disaster on disaster, woe to you, the declaration of the Lord GOD —
you built yourself a brothel-mound. You raised your platform in every public square.
On every street corner you built your platform. You turned your beauty into a disgrace. You spread your legs for every passerby. Your whoring multiplied.
You whored with the Egyptians — your big-bodied neighbors. You doubled your prostitution to provoke me.

So I stretched out my hand against you. I cut back your portion. I handed you over to the lust of those who hated you — the daughters of the Philistines — and even they were scandalized by your shameless behavior.
You whored with Assyria too — because you couldn't get enough. You whored with them and still weren't satisfied.
You took your whoring all the way to Chaldea, to the merchant land — and even that didn't fill you up.
How sick is your heart? — the declaration of the Lord GOD — that you do all this, the work of a brazen prostitute,
building your mound at every street corner, raising your platform in every square — and yet you weren't even like a prostitute, because you sneered at payment.
An adulterous wife! Taking strangers instead of her husband!
Every prostitute gets paid. But you — you handed out the gifts. You bribed your lovers to come from everywhere for your whoring.
You're the opposite of every other prostitute. No one chases you — you chase them. No one pays you — you pay them. You are inside-out.
So, whore — hear the word of the LORD.

This is what the Lord GOD says: Because your lust was poured out, your nakedness exposed in your whoring with your lovers, and because of every disgusting idol, and the blood of your children that you gave them —

watch. I'm gathering every lover you ever pleasured — every one you loved, every one you hated. I'm gathering them against you from every direction. I'm stripping you naked in front of them. They will see all of you.
I'll sentence you the way adulterers and murderers are sentenced. I'll bring on you the blood of fury and jealousy.
I'll hand you over to them. They'll tear down your mound. They'll smash your platform. They'll strip the clothes off you. They'll take your beautiful jewelry. They'll leave you naked and bare.
They'll bring a mob against you. They'll stone you. They'll hack you to pieces with their swords.
They'll burn your houses down and execute judgment on you while a crowd of women watches. I will end your whoring. There will be no more payments going out from you.
Then my fury will rest. My jealousy will leave you. I will be quiet. I will not be angry anymore.

Because you didn't remember the days of your youth — because you provoked me with all of this — I'm bringing your own path down on your head. The declaration of the Lord GOD. Did you not add this filth to all your other obscenities?
Everyone who uses proverbs will use this one against you: Like mother, like daughter.

You are your mother's daughter — a woman who despised her husband and her children. You are the sister of your sisters, who despised their husbands and their children. Your mother was a Hittite. Your father was an Amorite.
Your older sister is Samaria, living with her daughters to the north of you. Your younger sister is Sodom, living with her daughters to the south.
You didn't just walk in their ways and do their obscenities — that was too little for you. In every way, you went further into corruption than they did.
As I live — the declaration of the Lord GOD — your sister Sodom and her daughters never did what you and your daughters have done.
Listen — this was Sodom's guilt: she and her daughters had pride, full stomachs, comfortable peace — and they did not lift a finger for the poor and needy.
They became arrogant. They did detestable things in front of me. So I removed them — as you have seen.
Samaria didn't commit half your sins. You have done more disgusting things than they did. You make your sisters look righteous by comparison.

So bear your disgrace. You're the one who argued your sisters' case — and your own sins have made them look better than you. You made them look righteous. So burn with shame. Carry your humiliation. You made your sisters look innocent.
But I will restore them — Sodom and her daughters, Samaria and her daughters — and I will restore you along with them.
So you'll bear your shame and be humiliated by everything you did — and your shame will be a comfort to them.

Your sister Sodom and her daughters will return to what they were before. Samaria and her daughters will return to what they were before. And you and your daughters will return to what you were before.
You wouldn't even speak Sodom's name in the day of your arrogance —
before your own evil was exposed. Now you're the one being scorned — by the daughters of Aram and her neighbors, by the daughters of the Philistines, by everyone around you who despises you.
You will carry the weight of your obscenities and your disgusting acts. The declaration of the LORD.
This is what the Lord GOD says: I will do to you what you did — you despised the oath, you broke the covenant.
But I — I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth. I will establish with you a covenant that lasts forever.
Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your sisters — the older and the younger. I will give them to you as daughters, though not because of your covenant.
I will establish my covenant with you. And you will know — I am the LORD.

You will remember. You will be ashamed. You will never open your mouth again because of your humiliation — when I make atonement for you, for everything you have done. The declaration of the Lord GOD.

com.d:
# Ezekiel 16: The Difficult Love of God

This chapter narrates a love story twisted into heartbreak—God's unflinching account of Israel's unfaithfulness told through the metaphor of a foundling child rescued and clothed, then later utterly defiled by infidelity. The spiritual heart here is devastating and essential: God does not minimize sin, yet His love persists even through exposure of our deepest shame.

Ezekiel's opening frames Israel as an abandoned newborn, left unwashed in blood on the day of birth. God passes by and raises this helpless child into a beautiful woman, adorning her with fine linen and jewelry. This poetic reversal of fortune illustrates the extravagant grace of God's choosing love—undeserved, generous, and entirely His initiative. But then comes the reckoning. The favored bride turns prostitute, not merely committing infidelity but paying *others* to reject her, compounding her humiliation with willful degradation.

What makes this passage spiritually vital is that God refuses to look away from Israel's betrayal or soften its description. He names it plainly: idolatry, injustice, bloodshed, the exploitation of the vulnerable. There is no enabling here, no pretense that sin doesn't matter. Yet even in judgment, God's love is not retracted—it is grieved. The passage concludes with a promise of restoration: God will remember His covenant and establish an everlasting relationship, not on Israel's merit but on His mercy alone.

This speaks directly to our condition. We are all like Judah—rescued by grace, clothed in Christ's righteousness, yet prone to squandering our inheritance on lesser lovers: ambition, comfort, approval, false saviors. The text refuses us the luxury of self-deception. Our unfaithfulness matters profoundly. Yet the same God who names our sin with clarity remains committed to our restoration.

What patterns of unfaithfulness has God been patient enough to reveal in your own life? How might His willingness to speak truth be itself an expression of His covenant love?
com.s:
Ezekiel 16 stands as one of the most extended and graphic allegorical narratives in prophetic literature, comprising sixty-three verses that trace Jerusalem's history from infancy through apostasy to eventual restoration. Composed during the Babylonian exile, likely between 593 and 571 BCE, this chapter addresses the exiled community's need to comprehend why Jerusalem fell. Ezekiel employs the marriage metaphor common in prophetic discourse, yet extends it with unprecedented detail and shocking imagery that has generated considerable interpretive discussion across centuries of reception.

The foundational metaphor presents Jerusalem as an abandoned infant of mixed Amorite and Hittite parentage, emphasizing the city's pre-Israelite Canaanite origins and theological illegitimacy apart from divine election. The Hebrew term *mĕkōrōtayik* (your origin) in verse 3 denotes ancestral lineage, underscoring that Israel possessed no inherent claim to covenant blessing. YHWH's discovery of the blood-covered newborn and command to live (*ḥăyî*, an emphatic imperative repeated for emphasis in verse 6) establishes the relationship as purely gracious initiative. The subsequent adorning with fine garments, jewelry, and royal status (verses 10–14) employs wedding and coronation imagery drawn from ancient Near Eastern royal conventions.

The chapter's central section (verses 15–34) details Jerusalem's unfaithfulness through the term *taznût* (prostitution/whoring), which appears with striking frequency throughout. Scholarly debate surrounds whether the sexual imagery refers primarily to political alliances with Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon, or to syncretistic worship practices, though the text likely encompasses both dimensions. The comparison with Sodom and Samaria (verses 44–58) employs a lesser-to-greater argument, declaring Jerusalem's sins exceeded those of proverbially wicked cities—a rhetorical strategy designed to demolish any residual self-righteousness among the exiles.

The concluding verses introduce the critical term *bĕrît ʿôlām* (everlasting covenant) in verse 60, pointing toward restoration grounded not in Israel's faithfulness but in divine commitment. This tension between devastating judgment and ultimate restoration reflects the broader prophetic pattern wherein covenant curses serve redemptive purposes. The chapter's canonical placement between chapters 15 and 17, both employing vine imagery, creates a triptych examining Jerusalem's failed vocation, with chapter 16 providing the theological and emotional center of this indictment.
com.p:
Ezekiel chapter sixteen stands as one of the most devastating and tender passages in all prophetic literature, delivered approximately 593 to 571 years before the incarnation of Christ, during the darkest hour of Judah's exile in Babylon. The prophet speaks while Jerusalem still stands but totters toward her final destruction in 586 BC. This extended allegory arrives after the northern kingdom has already fallen to Assyria and while the southern kingdom drinks the dregs of her own unfaithfulness. Within redemptive history, this passage belongs to the era of exile and judgment, that painful season when God's covenant discipline fell upon His people for their persistent idolatry, yet even here the seeds of restoration whisper through the ruins.

The allegory presents Jerusalem as an abandoned infant, cast out at birth with umbilical cord uncut, unwashed, and left to die in her blood—a picture of utter helplessness and defilement representing Israel's origins among the Canaanite peoples before any covenant existed. The Lord passed by and spoke life over this dying child: "Live!" This sovereign word of grace transformed a rejected foundling into a royal bride adorned with embroidered cloth, fine leather, linen, silk, gold, silver, and a crown of beauty. Here shimmers the typological pattern of divine election and unmerited favor that reaches its fullest expression in Christ's love for His church, the bride He found dead in trespasses and sins and raised to sit with Him in heavenly places.

Yet Jerusalem's grotesque betrayal forms the chapter's agonizing center. She took the very gifts of her Bridegroom—the gold, silver, oil, and fine flour—and fashioned them into instruments of spiritual adultery, offering them to false gods and even sacrificing her children, those who belonged to the Lord, in the fires of Molech. The prophetic indictment escalates as God declares Jerusalem worse than Sodom and Samaria, her sister cities in shame. This was fulfilled in the Babylonian destruction that reduced the temple to ashes and scattered the covenant people among the nations.

Yet the chapter does not end in judgment. The Lord remembers His covenant and promises to establish an everlasting covenant, a promise that reaches across centuries to find its fulfillment in the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood. The church now lives as the restored bride, clothed not in her own righteousness but in garments washed white, awaiting the marriage supper of the Lamb when shame shall be swallowed in eternal glory.
